newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam congratulates China on Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam congratulates China on Hong Kong handover.

text.p: Vietnam's leaders have congratulated their Chinese counterparts on the handover of Hong Kong, hailing it as the end of more than 100 years of domination, official media reports said on Monday.

"They said in a joint message signed on Saturday that Tuesday July 1, 1997 'will enter into China's history as a great event, marking the end of foreign domination over Hong Kong for more than 100 years'," the daily Vietnam News said.

It said Hanoi believed the "one-country, two systems" plan, Hong Kong's high level of autonomy and the concept of Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong would ensure stability and development for the former British colony.
"These guidelines conform with the aspirations of Chinese people from the mainland and in Hong Kong, and aspirations for regional peace and development," it said.
Hanoi's leaders added that Vietnam paid a lot of attention to strengthening and expanding relations and cooperation with Chinese people on the mainland and in Hong Kong.

Vietnam is a neighbour and ideological ally of China, but relations have not always been good. Earlier this year they came under strain again, when China started drilling for gas in a South China Sea area Vietnam claims as its own.
After a brief diplomatic spat, the Chinese drilling rig was moved out of the contested waters.

The message -- from the leadership troika of Communist Party chief, president and prime minister and the National Assembly chairman -- did not mention the thorny issue of Vietnamese boatpeople who will be left in Hong Kong after the handover.
Vietnam took a swipe last week at British Hong Kong over delays in repatriating some of the last boatpeople.
A foreign ministry statement put the blame for the failure of efforts to deport 430 people before the handover deadline squarely at the feet of the colonial administration and London.
The statement referred to the return of a group of boatpeople which, for a variety of reasons -- including medical and legal -- has been delayed.

Vietnam's boatpeople are a legacy of the Vietnam War, which ended in 1975 with the fall of the government of U.S.-backed Saigon to Hanoi's forces. In the years that followed, hundreds of thousands left their homeland for countries around the region.

Repatriation efforts began in the late 1980s, and since then most asylum camps in the region have been emptied. But despite Chinese objections, around 3,200 Vietnamese will still be in Hong Kong on its return to mainland sovereignty.

Among those are some 1,600 people who are waiting for resettlement in third countries as refugees, 800 recent arrivals who will be deported later, 397 of whom Vietnam has not recognised as its own nationals and the 430 now in dispute.
Although the issue will continue to be handled by Hong Kong authorities after the handover, Britain's responsibility will end once the Union Jack is lowered over Victoria Harbour.
Analysts say the matter could become a future point of friction between Hanoi and Hong Kong's new Beijing masters.
